concepts.def: The tissue that covers the outer surfaces of a plant. In a leaf it forms the upper and lower epidermis, a protective covering that contains the guard cells surrounding the stomata.
The leaf tissue lying just below the upper epidermis. Its closely packed cells contain many chloroplasts, so this is the main tissue in which photosynthesis takes place.
The leaf tissue lying below the palisade mesophyll. Its cells are loosely packed with air spaces between them, so gases can diffuse to and from the photosynthesising cells.
Plant tissue found at the growing tips of shoots and roots. Its cells divide to produce the new cells a plant needs for growth.

The tissue that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves. It is composed of hollow tubes strengthened by lignin, adapted for the transport of water in the transpiration stream.

The tissue that transports dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage. It is composed of tubes of elongated cells, and cell sap can move from one phloem cell to the next through pores in the end walls.
The movement of food molecules, as dissolved sugars, through phloem tissue from the leaves to the rest of the plant.

Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from a plant, which diffuses out of the leaves through the stomata. The transpiration stream is the movement of water taken up by the roots and carried up through the xylem to the stems and leaves that replaces it.
A cell on the outside of a root, drawn out into a long thin hair that gives a large surface area. It is adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis and of mineral ions by active transport.
A stoma is a pore in the epidermis of a leaf. Each stoma is surrounded by a pair of guard cells that open and close it. The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss.
The roots, stem and leaves, which work together as an organ system for the transport of substances around the plant.

mcqs.q: What does xylem tissue transport, and in which direction?
options: Dissolved sugars, from the leaves to all parts
Water and mineral ions, from the roots to leaves
Cell sap, from each living cell to the next one
Mineral ions, drawn into the roots by osmosis
mcqs.explain: Xylem tissue transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stems and leaves, carrying the water in the transpiration stream.

mcqs.q: How does a root hair cell take up water and mineral ions from the soil?
options: Water enters by osmosis and ions by active transport
Water and mineral ions both enter the cell by osmosis
Water enters by osmosis and sugars by translocation
Water enters through pores in the cells' end walls
mcqs.explain: Root hair cells are adapted for the efficient uptake of water by osmosis, and mineral ions by active transport.

options: Water and mineral ions move up to the leaves
Dissolved sugars move to the rest of the plant
Cell sap moves through tubes stiffened by lignin
Water and mineral ions enter cells by osmosis
mcqs.explain: Translocation is the movement of food molecules through phloem tissue, carrying dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant for immediate use or storage.

mcqs.q: What is the role of the guard cells that surround each stoma?
options: They control gas exchange and water loss from the leaf
They are the pores through which gases pass in or out
They open more widely when the surrounding air is humid
They hold the air spaces in which photosynthesis occurs
mcqs.explain: The role of stomata and guard cells is to control gas exchange and water loss, the guard cells opening and closing each pore.

mcqs.q: A potted plant is moved from a cool, shaded room with still, humid air into a warm, brightly lit room with moving, dry air. What happens to its rate of transpiration?
options: It decreases, as the drier air holds less water vapour
It decreases, as the moving air cools the leaf surface
It stays the same, as the same volume of water is lost
It increases, as water evaporates and diffuses faster
mcqs.explain: Higher temperature, higher light intensity, greater air movement and lower humidity each increase the rate of transpiration: the stomata open in the light and water vapour diffuses out of them more quickly.

mcqs.q: A student measured the water lost by three identical shoots. Shoot A lost 1.2 cm3 in 60 minutes in still air at 20 degrees C. Shoot B lost 2.4 cm3 in 60 minutes in moving air at 20 degrees C. Shoot C lost 2.0 cm3 in 40 minutes in still air at 30 degrees C. Which conclusion do the results support?
options: The highest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C
The lowest rate of water loss was in moving air at 20 C
The highest rate of water loss was in still air at 30 C
Still air at 20 C gave the highest rate of water loss
mcqs.explain: Rate of transpiration is volume divided by time: shoot C lost 2.0 cm3 in 40 minutes, which is 0.05 cm3 per minute, higher than shoot B at 0.04 and shoot A at 0.02.

mcqs.q: How is the structure of palisade mesophyll related to its function in a leaf?
options: Its cells are spread apart to let gases move around
Its cells are hollow tubes made stronger by lignin
Its cells contain many chloroplasts that absorb light
Its cells are one tissue that forms the whole leaf
mcqs.explain: Palisade mesophyll cells are packed with chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf, so the tissue is structured to absorb light for photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Which statement describes the process of transpiration?
options: Sugars dissolve in cells and move down through the xylem
Water passes out through the guard cells acting as pores
Water vapour moves back into the leaf from the humid air
Water evaporates from cells and diffuses out of stomata
mcqs.explain: In transpiration water evaporates from the cells inside the leaf and the water vapour diffuses out through the stomata, and the water lost is replaced by the transpiration stream in the xylem.
